Fitting the Models to Participant Data

Participants in the TAMBI mosquito defense task face a complex learning problem: they must infer hidden environmental regularities (latent state transitions, cue-dependent directional offsets, and the distinction between noise and genuine change) from noisy, intermittent outcome feedback. Not all participants approach this problem in the same way. Some may engage in latent structure inference, tracking hidden states and attributing surprises to their appropriate sources. Others may rely on simpler strategies: following the most recent outcome direction, learning the association between cue colours and attack directions without ever building a model of the latent state dynamics, or covering all structured attack locations without inferring which state is currently active. A small number may not engage meaningfully at all.

. This is essential for three reasons:

The six parameters of the inference agent (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility, cue sensitivity, placement noise) are defined within a latent-structure-learning agent. Estimating these parameters for a participant who is not performing structure learning would be scientifically inappropriate (analogous to fitting a linear regression model to non-linear data).

Participants who clicked randomly or without meaningful engagement should be identified and excluded from subsequent analyses. Here, model comparison provides an objective, data-driven exclusion criterion.
Characterisation of the learning strategy spectrum.

The distribution of winning models across participants provides insight into the prevalence of different learning strategies in the sample, and can be related to instruction condition and trait-level measures.

(Radev et al., 2023; Schmitt et al., 2023) to perform amortized Bayesian model comparison. The approach follows the same simulation-based inference logic as the parameter estimation pipeline: a neural classifier is trained on a large corpus of simulated behavioral data (generated from all candidate models), and then applied to real participant data to estimate posterior model probabilities.

Compared with model comparison by information criteria or by Bayes factors obtained with bridge sampling, both of which require a tractable likelihood that the present simulators do not have, amortized model comparison:
Operates on the same 54 behavioral summary features used for parameter estimation (ensuring consistency)
Returns posterior probabilities over models, whose calibration can be checked on simulated data
Requires no per-participant optimization or sampling at inference time
Can be validated via confusion matrices, calibration curves, and model recovery analyses before application to real data

The posterior model probabilities are conditional on the candidate set and on the prior over each model’s parameters. They state which of the five candidate models best accounts for a participant’s feature vector, and they do not state that this model describes the participant well in absolute terms. That question is addressed by the

Rather than comparing a large number of models that differ in subtle ways, we define a compact set of five models that span the qualitative spectrum from disengaged behavior to full latent structure inference. Each successive model adds a qualitatively distinct cognitive capability.

The rationale for limiting the set to these models is twofold. First, the cognitive transitions (no learning → outcome tracking → cue association → knowledge of the four structured locations → state inference) capture the most important qualitative distinctions in learning strategy. Second, model variants that differ only in continuous parameter settings within the structure-learning agent (e.g. with or without oddball attribution, with fixed or free volatility) are better handled by the parameter estimation pipeline, where these differences manifest as different parameter values rather than as discrete model classes. Maintaining them as separate models would test the same cognitive dimension at both the model and the parameter level.

processes the feature vector, reshaped to a 1-element set, and maps the 54-dimensional feature vector to an 8-dimensional embedding. With a single set element, the DeepSet is functionally an MLP encoder.
An MLP with two hidden layers of 64 units each (SiLU activation, no dropout) maps the 8-dimensional embedding to 5 logits, which are passed through a softmax to produce posterior model probabilities.
The network is deliberately small relative to the 40,000 training simulations, given the low complexity of a five-class classification problem on 54 features.

children.value: Misclassification has direct consequences for participant exclusion and for the interpretation of subsequent parameter estimates. Five complementary validation analyses are run by
, and their numerical results are written to
. All numbers below are taken from that file for the current five-model classifier.

The validation set comprises 4,000 simulations, 800 per model, generated with fresh parameter draws on the same 20 trial schedules that were used for training. All five analyses are closed-world checks: they establish that the classifier separates the five models when the data were generated by one of them, and they do not establish how the classifier behaves on data that none of the five models generated.
For each simulation, the classifier predicts the model with the highest posterior probability. Overall accuracy was 0.99875, corresponding to 5 misclassifications in 4,000 simulations.

5.6 What the validation does not cover

children.label: 5.6 What the validation does not cover

children.value: Near-perfect closed-world accuracy shows that the five simulators occupy almost non-overlapping regions of the 54-dimensional feature space. It also means that the classifier has seen almost no ambiguous cases during training, so that its output for a feature vector that lies between or outside these regions is an extrapolation. Three checks are therefore outstanding before the posterior model probabilities of real participants can be taken at face value: a test of whether participants’ feature vectors lie within the simulated feature distribution (model misspecification in summary space; Schmitt et al., 2023), the comparison with action noise matched across models described in Section 2.6, and the stability of the participant classification across independently trained classifiers. 7. Relation to the Instruction Condition Manipulation

children.label: 7. Relation to the Instruction Condition Manipulation

children.value: The three instruction conditions differ in what participants are told about the structure before the task (see
Participants are told how to place nets and must discover all regularities through experience.
Participants are additionally told that rules might determine the attack direction, without being told what the rules are.
Participants are additionally told the cue offset (about 70°) and the rotation of both directions (about 120°) at irregular intervals.

The distribution of the model classes across the three conditions serves as a manipulation check, namely whether instruction shifts participants toward strategies that use more of the task structure. This distribution has not yet been computed for the five-model classifier (see Section 6.3).
